newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan hangs best-selling prison writer, 3 others.
newsitem.headline: Japan hangs best-selling prison writer, 3 others.

text.p: Japan has executed four people, including a best-selling prison author whose death sentence for murders committed while a minor sparked a national debate on capital punishment, media reported on Saturday.

Norio Nagayama, 48, a former coffee shop employee convicted of killing four people in a 1968 shooting spree, and Hideki Kanda, 54, who slayed his father and two others with a sword in 1985, were hanged in Tokyo, Kyodo news agency and major daily newspapers said.

At a detention centre in the northern city of Sapporo, mining subcontractor Yasumasa Hidaka, 54, and his wife Nobuko, 51, were hanged for killing six of their employees in a 1984 dormitory fire they set to receive insurance, the reports said.

The reports of the executions, which took place on Friday and were Japan's first since last December, were attributed to "prison sources" because the Justice Ministry does not announce or confirm executions.

The Justice Ministry's long-standing policy, which capital punishment critics say adds to the cruelty of the death penalty, is to make no announcement of when hangings are to take place or say why certain convicts are selected and not others.
Witnesses are not allowed, and the only way the public finds out is through the executed person's family, who are served with blunt notices to collect the bodies.

The case of Nagayama, who stole a handgun from a U.S. military base and shot to death two security guards and two taxi drivers across Japan in a one-month spree when he was 19 years old, sparked a fierce debate about whether crimes committed by minors should be subject to the death penalty.
People in Japan are considered minors until the age of 20.

Some analysts said Nagayama's execution, which came as Japan was reeling from a pair of grisly killings by a 14-year-old schoolboy, was a message from justice authorities that they will not be lenient on murderous youths.
Nagayama was arrested in 1969 and first sentenced to death in 1979 by the Tokyo District Court in a ruling the Tokyo High Court later commuted to life in prison.

In July 1983, the Supreme Court, ordered the high court to retry Nagayama, whose death penalty was reinstated in 1987. The Supreme Court rejected Nagayama's appeal against the ruling and his death sentence was finalised in 1990.
Nagayama began writing novels and poems while in prison, producing a best seller in 1971 and winning an award for new writers in 1983.
The hanging of the four convicts brought to 25 the number of death row inmates executed since 1993, when Japan resumed executions after a hiatus of more than three years.
Japan had stopped executions in November 1989, raising a glimmer of hope among abolitionists that it would stop the practice.
Japan has hanged more than 580 people since 1945. Abolitionists believe there are currently more than 50 convicts on death row.
